newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Foreign oil firms rushing to explore Mozambique.
newsitem.headline: Foreign oil firms rushing to explore Mozambique.

text.p: International oil companies, attracted by vast unexplored areas and world class gas finds, are flocking to Mozambique with several already active in one of the world's poorest countries.
Analysts and diplomats said Mozambique, just emerging from 16 years of civil war which all but destroyed its economy, held great promise -- particularly in gas.
It already boasts world class gas reserves at the Pande and Temane fields and companies already active in the southern African country have reported promising signs.
Pande's proven reserves are 2.5-3.0 trillion cubic feet (tcf) while the Temane field has proven reserves of 0.6 tcf but estimates of the field stretch to 2 tcf.
South Africa's JCI Ltd has announced plans to build an iron ore reduction plant in Mozambique utilising gas from Pande or Temane fields.
Two years ago, almost no oil companies were involved in exploration in Mozambique -- one of the poorest countries in the world according to the World Bank.

But since the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Maputo government and U.S. oil company Enron Corp in late 1995, exploration and/or production sharing contracts have been awarded on 10 blocks covering the whole of Mozambique's sedimentary area.
Pande is being developed by Enron together with state-owned ENH-Hidrocarbonetos De Mocambique.
The U.S. embassy said the rush for exploration permits in less than two years have been impressive.

"The flurry of exploration and production sharing contracts the past 20 months has been impressive...The involvement of major companies makes real the possibility of an oil and gas industry in Mozambique," the U.S Embassy in Mozambique said in a recent report.

Eloi Dolivo of Geneva-based analysts Petroconsultants said at least 10 foreign oil companies were active in Mozambique. Nine of them had signed MoU's with the Mozambique government and Canadian company Canop was about to sign a MoU for the Xai-Xai block -- covering about 38,000 square km north of Maputo.
"It is nothing like Western Siberia yet. But who knows?"
The promise of gas and maybe oil in Mozambique has already attracted majors like Atlantic Richfield Co (Arco), The British Petroleum Co Plc and Enron.
South Africa's Sasol Ltd and Lonrhopet -- a division of Lonrho Plc -- were also involved in Mozambique.
Several junior oil companies, like Canop, Scimitar Hydrocarbons Corp, Leopardus Resources Ltd, Antrium and Norbay Oil were actively exploring in the country.
BP said last year that although no commercial oil had been found in Mozambique, only four wells have been drilled.
BP currently has exclusive rights to explore an offshore area up to 40,000 square km in Mozambique's Zambezi delta.

"Though BP is clearly looking for oil, the existence of other major players in the area helps make a gas find for them viable since it could be combined with gas from other fields to supply larger projects, like liquefied natural gas, or transported to a developing South African market through existing pipelines," the U.S. embassy report said.
Dolivo said other foreign companies were interested in BP's leftovers.
"The Malaysian state company Petronas and Triton (Energy Ltd) separately are mooted as (being) interested by the area BP will release upon termination of its MoU period," Dolivo said.
-- Johannesburg newsroom, +27-11 482-1003
